sections.h2: What the Washtenaw County deed office holds
sections.html:
Land research in Washtenaw County runs through the Register of Deeds. Its files include deeds, mortgages and foreclosure records, along with other real and personal property papers. The register works inside the joint Clerk / Register of Deeds department, and inspection is open to all comers.

The office's main page links to recording rules, record searches and requests, eRecording, a fee schedule and a transfer tax explainer. Copies bought through the online land record search need a login.

Recording finishes a sale, because the buyer is shielded from later claimants only once the deed is on file. Closings usually pass the signed deed to a title company, which can tell you the recording date and supply a recorded copy for your files.

sections.h2: Can a deed be filed electronically?
sections.html:
Yes. Electronic filings come in through vendors approved by the Register of Deeds, a route lenders and title agents rely on. An owner who signs outside a title closing usually files on paper, mailing it or visiting the counter in Ann Arbor.

Read the recording requirements page before you send anything, since a paper with layout defects comes back unrecorded. The fee schedule page lists what the county charges for each service.

  • Keep the original signed deed in hand until the county accepts it.
  • Ask which payment types the office takes for your kind of filing.
  • Request your recorded deed before listing, so the buyer's title agent has the legal description early.

sections.h2: Recording fees and transfer tax rates
sections.html:
Michigan statutes supply the baseline figures for any register of deeds, and the county applies them. Each charge below is paired with its section, and you can read the text at the Michigan Legislature site.

sections.h2: Who pays transfer tax, and what avoids it
sections.html:
The tax lands on the seller. MCL 207.523 makes the grantor liable and sets a 15-day window, running from delivery of the deed, for payment to the county treasurer. The county's explainer adds a rule that trips people up. Collection is automatic unless the deed qualifies and states the reason on its face.

So any exemption you intend to use has to be written into the deed. MCL 207.526 lists the categories, including:

  • Spouses creating or ending a tenancy by the entireties.
  • A parent or grandparent deeding to a child, stepchild, adopted child or grandchild.
  • A boundary line correction where no money changes hands.
  • A joint tenancy in which one co-owner already holds title.
  • A deed given through foreclosure or as a substitute for it.

A payer who later learns that an exemption applied can request a refund from the state Treasury department under subsection (4) of the section on liability.

sections.h2: Does a warranty deed need a tax certificate?
sections.html:
Usually. MCL 211.135 has registers of deeds ask for treasurer certificates whenever a deed or land contract is presented. They disclose tax liens or tax titles and confirm that the five years of tax before the instrument date were paid.

A quitclaim deed carrying no warranty covenants gets a pass, and so do sheriff's deeds and a handful of other types. If you are signing an ordinary warranty deed, line up the certificate first.

When back tax is owed, the county treasurer will quote a payoff. Pay it by closing and the certificate follows, which lets the deed go to the recorder without delay.

Format rules are in MCL 565.201, and a register must refuse any paper that breaks them. Check these before anyone signs.

  • Line one of the printed text names the one recordable event, for instance warranty deed.
  • Black ink on white stock of 20-pound weight or heavier, with type no smaller than 10 points.
  • 2 1/2 inches blank above the text on page one and half an inch on every remaining edge.
  • A mailing address for each grantee, and the drafter's name with a business address.
  • Social Security numbers trimmed to the final four digits.
  • A stapled English translation on any paper written partly in another language.

The office also enrolls people in Fraud Guard alerts, which warn you when a paper is recorded under your name. It is a sensible precaution while a house sits listed or vacant. Two other county pages cover older paperwork: discharging prohibited deed restrictions, such as covenants that discriminated by race or religion, and the Michigan Construction Lien Act, which matters if contractors recently worked on the house.

1. Ask the title company whether your deed is a warranty or a quitclaim, since that decides whether a treasurer's certificate is needed.
  2. Get a payoff figure from the Washtenaw County Treasurer if any tax is owing.
  3. Decide whether an exemption applies and make sure the deed states the reason on its face.
  4. Check the format rules before signing, with the first line naming the recordable event.
  5. Pay transfer tax to the county treasurer within 15 days of delivering the deed if the closing agent is not collecting it.
  6. Ask for the recorded copy so your own files show the recording date.

A cash sale skips the lender's paperwork, but not the recording steps, so the same list applies. Bring the parcel number and the legal description to any call with the office, since staff will ask for one or the other. If the title company is handling everything, ask for a short written timeline that shows who files the deed and who pays the tax, and keep it with your closing papers.

sections.h2: Washtenaw County homes and local offices
sections.html:
Ann Arbor is the county seat. Chelsea, Dexter, Manchester, Saline, Ypsilanti and the northern slice of Milan are the other cities, with Barton Hills a village and Whitmore Lake a census community. Main roads are I-94, US 23, US 12, M-14, M-17 and M-52.

The county has 165,103 housing units, and owners occupy 61.6 percent of homes. The middle owner-occupied value is $374,100. Typical household income is $89,180 and typical gross rent is $1,463. Zoning, building permits and assessing belong to local units, so ask the city or township about any open permit before you list.

faqs.q: Does Washtenaw County take electronic deed filings?
faqs.a: Yes. Lenders and title companies commonly file through eRecording vendors that the Register of Deeds has approved.

faqs.q: Who is responsible for transfer tax in a Washtenaw County sale?
faqs.a: The seller. Michigan sets 55 cents for the county plus $3.75 for the state on each $500 of value, and the county treasurer must receive payment within 15 days after the deed is delivered.

faqs.q: Does my Washtenaw County deed have to name a transfer tax exemption?
faqs.a: Yes. The tax is collected unless the instrument is exempt and the exemption appears on the face of the deed, so write out the statutory reason before signing.

faqs.q: What tax paperwork goes with a Washtenaw County warranty deed?
faqs.a: Certificates from the county treasurer showing no tax liens or titles and five prior years of paid taxes. A quitclaim deed with no warranty covenants is excused.

faqs.q: Where can I confirm the Washtenaw County recording fee?
faqs.a: Check the Register of Deeds fee schedule page, which covers recording, copies, searches, transfer tax and tax certificates. State law sets the starting recording charge at $30.00 per document.
